title: Segregated service lanes: Terraform module for subnet groups, NAT/IGW failover, and endpoint policies
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary:
Implement a reusable Terraform module that defines 'segregated service lanes' — logically grouped subnets and associated infrastructure patterns for private VPC deployments. The module will provide first-class support for: subnet group templates (control/management, public edge, service-worker, db/storage), multi-AZ NAT gateway provisioning with automated failover, IGW attachment patterns for public lanes, VPC endpoint creation for S3/Dynamo/RDS and custom service endpoints, and an opinionated routing policy that prefers intra-VPC private paths and falls back to NAT/IGW using health-checked route priorities.

Motivation:
Customers deploying Redwood Private need a predictable, secure default topology that: (1) partitions workloads by trust/routability; (2) makes upgrades and lifecycle predictable (module versions + safe drift policy); and (3) reduces incidents caused by misrouted egress when a NAT gateway or AZ fails. Current infra repos have ad-hoc templates and operational pain around NAT failover, endpoint policies, and route reconciliation. This module centralizes patterns and telemetry hooks so Platform Ops can observe and remediate network health quicker.

Scope and non-goals:
- In scope: Terraform 1.5-compatible module; variables for CIDR themes, AZ counts, subnet sizing strategy, enablement toggles for NAT high-availability vs single-NAT (cost trade-off), VPC endpoint allowlist, route table tagging, cloud-provider-specific health-checking (AWS route53/ENI probe integration), outputs for subnets/route-tables/endpoint-IDs, and lightweight reconciliation scripts (optional) to run as CI job.
- Out of scope: Application-level firewall rules, service mesh config, and platform-specific VM provisioning. The module will not embed SSM/user-data or bootstrap scripts.

Design highlights and trade-offs:
1) Subnet group model: expose a small set of semantic lanes (public-edge, private-services, private-workers, management). Each lane maps to one or more subnet "slots" per AZ. This keeps the API simple compared to free-form subnet lists.
2) NAT failover: prefer multiple AutoScale NAT Gateways across AZs + route priorities using Cloud Provider route weights where possible. For providers that cannot weight routes, implement a small healthcheck lambda (or cloud function) that updates route attachment to the healthiest NAT ENI. Tradeoff: additional slight complexity vs deterministic failover.
3) Endpoint policies: create both interface and gateway endpoints with tight IAM/endpoint policy templates and option to supply a JSON policy override. Default policy will allow access only to Redwood-managed service principals and S3 from private-services lanes.
4) Upgrade strategy: support a two-stage module upgrade pattern: (a) plan-only CI stage that runs terraform plan and static checks, (b) canary apply to a single tenant VPC via a gated pipeline, (c) staggered rollout across remaining VPCs. Include Terraform state locking and a recommended destroy_protection flag for sensitive route tables.

Health checks and observability:
- Export three core metrics to our internal telemetry (via CloudWatch metrics or provider equivalents): NAT-attachment-health (per-AZ), Endpoint-Policy-violations (count of denied flows logged), and Route-Reconciliation-ops (count of automated route swaps).
- The module will create lightweight CloudWatch Events / EventBridge rules to emit events on route flips and endpoint lifecycle changes to the central ops SNS topic.
- Provide optional synthetic probe resource that periodically issues small egress requests (to an allowed external probe target) routed through each NAT path to surface latency and failure.

Upgrade and rollback plan:
- Planned minor release path: bump module version, run plan against a staging tenant, validate endpoint stability and NAT failover via synthetic probes, run canary apply to a single low-traffic tenant, monitor metrics for 48h, then proceed with bulk apply.
- For a failed canary: automatic rollback instructions provided in the runbook; route reconciliation script can be run to revert to last-known-good NAT attachments.

Runbooks and acceptance testing:
- Include a playground terraform example that spins a 3-AZ VPC with all lanes and endpoints enabled and sample application security groups.
- Add a suite of acceptance tests (Terratest or kitchen-terraform) to validate: subnet allocations, cross-AZ NAT failover, endpoint connectivity from private lanes, and route tag consistency.

APIs (Terraform module variables & outputs):
- Variables (high-level): cidr_block, az_count, lanes (map of lane -> prefix_length), nat_ha (bool), enable_gateway_endpoints (bool), enable_interface_endpoints (list), endpoint_policy_json (string override), route_health_check_enabled (bool), tags (map).
- Outputs: subnet_ids (map of lane -> list), route_table_ids (map), nat_gateway_ids (list), endpoint_ids (map), healthcheck_resources (list), module_version (string).

Security considerations:
- Default endpoint policies will be restrictive; ops must expressly opt-in to broader allowlists.
- Module will not create IAM roles with wildcard permissions. Any role created for healthcheck lambdas will use least privilege.

Acceptance criteria (high level):
- Terraform module compiles with Terraform 1.5 and runs a full apply in playground without errors.
- Synthetic probe demonstrates automatic re-route when NAT in an AZ is disabled.
- Endpoint policies are attached and deny unauthorized access; tests show only allowed principals can reach endpoints.
- Central telemetry receives NAT-attachment-health and route-change events within 60s of changes.
- Documentation and runbook uploaded to Confluence, and a sample canary pipeline recipe added to CD repo.
